Give meeting notes one internal record, so a source is a choice and not a fork (#561)

* Give meeting notes one internal record, so a source is a choice not a fork

Follows the direction set in #75: define the record first, and let provider
differences resolve into it rather than into conditionals spread through the
flows.

The record is the contract. Two decisions in it carry the weight.

**Absence is representable.** Titles and attendees are routinely empty from real
providers, because a recorder that titles and attributes from a calendar it
cannot read returns neither. A record that forced them would push adapters into
inventing values, and an invented attendee becomes an invented commitment two
steps later. Empty means unknown and callers must treat it so.

**Provenance is mandatory.** `source` and `source_id` are what dedup and
person-page touch tracking run on, so a record without them is reprocessed as
new on every sweep.

Two adapters ship together on purpose, because a contract fitted to one provider
is a shape drawn around that provider. Granola and Wispr disagree at nearly
every edge: one supplies a title, attendees with emails, and action items the
user has already curated as checkboxes; the other supplies no title, no
attendees, and action items as prose under a heading. Both produce the same
record and nothing downstream can tell them apart. Granola's behaviour is
unchanged. Completed checkboxes are deliberately not imported, since handing
someone back work they have finished is worse than missing it.

Attendance is resolved through the matcher Dex already ships. A capture that
matches a calendar entry gains real attendees and the real title; one that does
not keeps an explicit warning and records why, because no entry within the
window and a calendar that could not be read call for different responses. Three
refusals are tested, each of which would otherwise produce a confident false
statement about who was in a room: a derived title is never offered to the
matcher as corroboration, matching an event that lists nobody leaves attendance
unresolved, and a calendar that cannot be read is never reported as a meeting
with no attendees.

One trap worth recording for anyone calling that matcher: it parses timestamps
and rejects any that does not declare an offset, so passing a datetime object
rather than an ISO string makes every capture come back unmatched with reason
capture_timestamp_missing_timezone, which is indistinguishable from a genuinely
absent calendar entry.

Notes land in 00-Inbox/Meetings/ so the existing detector picks them up
unchanged, per the landing-zone contract. A guard fails the build if the record,
the attribution join, the landing zone or the calendar lookup ever names a
provider; it caught a docstring on its first run.

Routine analytics receipts evict the snapshots a user would actually rewind (#584)

`_prune_committed(keep=3)` runs on every commit and keeps the newest three
COMMITTED transactions with no awareness of what they are, so bookkeeping
competes on equal terms with the snapshots rewind depends on.

`analytics-receipt` is written for session_started, task_created, task_completed
and idea_implemented. On my vault: 3 receipts on 14 Aug, 30 on 17 Aug, 4 on the
18th, 13 on the 19th, 4 on the 20th. Three session opens is enough.

Measured: an update committed its snapshot at 00:38 and reported it present. By
09:33 the transaction directory held three entries, all `analytics-receipt`
written between 09:30 and 09:33 that morning, and the update's snapshot was gone.
Nobody did anything except open Dex.

`rewind_adoption` then refuses with "the adoption snapshot is no longer available
under keep-last-3 retention; this adoption can no longer be rewound", which reads
as a retention policy working as intended rather than telemetry having consumed
the budget.

/dex-update states the promise honestly -- "rewind remains available while its
snapshot is retained among the newest three" -- but a reader hears three
meaningful operations, not three analytics pings. The only retention signal the
API surfaces is warning_threshold_bytes at 2 GiB against 52 KB of real usage, so
the size warning can never fire while the thing that actually removes the
snapshot stays invisible.

This applies `keep` per class. Bookkeeping operations append their own small
receipt and hold nothing a user would ask to undo; they keep their own newest
three and can no longer evict an adoption or release snapshot.

The nightly checkup cannot find node, so no .cjs hook has been checked (#591)

* Give the nightly checkup a PATH that can find node

smoke.py syntax-checks Dex's .cjs hooks with node, and locates node on the
inherited PATH. launchd hands a scheduled job a minimal PATH containing
neither Homebrew prefix, so on a normal Mac node is invisible to the nightly
run even though it works in every terminal.

The result is not a failure anybody notices. The hooks journey returns
UNKNOWN rather than BROKEN, so it reads as "could not check" instead of
"hook checking has not run for months". On the vault this was found on, every
.cjs hook had gone unverified since early August.

The shipped plist template carried no EnvironmentVariables block at all, while
the other two shipped Launch Agents (changelog-checker, learning-review) both
set a PATH. Those two also predate Apple Silicon and list only /usr/local/bin.

Two changes, because one alone does not reach everybody:

- The template now sets a PATH including both Homebrew prefixes, so new
  installs are correct.
- nightly-smoke.sh widens PATH itself when node is not already reachable,
  which is what fixes installs that ALREADY exist: an update refreshes scripts
  but never rewrites an installed plist.

The worker resolves node the same defensive way it already resolves python a
few lines above. It appends rather than prepends, so anything already on PATH
keeps priority, and the validated-tool checks in release_channel.py still
decide what is safe to execute. This widens where node may be found, not what
is trusted.

Three tests, each of which fails on the unpatched tree.

* Hide node with an empty directory, not a system path

The test set PATH to "/usr/bin:/bin" to hide node so the worker's
fallback would be exercised. On a host that ships /usr/bin/node the
guard resolves node immediately, the fallback never runs, and the
assertion compares against the system binary instead of the fake
prefix. It fails there and asserts nothing anywhere.

An empty temporary directory hides node on every host. The block
under test uses only bash builtins and bash is invoked by absolute
path, so it needs nothing else on PATH.

Add Wispr Flow as a meeting source Dex can reach without a host (#562)

* Add Wispr Flow as a meeting source Dex can reach without a host

Builds on the internal meeting record. Wispr exposes meetings over a remote MCP
server behind a standards-compliant OAuth 2.1 authorization server, so the
credential does not have to live inside an MCP client's connector store. Held by
Dex, the same connection works from a scheduled job, from a different MCP
client, or from a plain script. That is the difference between a source that
works while someone is signed in and one that works overnight.

Three properties of this provider shape the design, and each caused a real
failure before it was understood:

- Access tokens live 300 seconds, so refresh is part of nearly every call rather
  than an occasional repair.
- The refresh token rotates on every use and the old one dies immediately, so
  the write is atomic and the previous credential survives until the replacement
  is durable. A torn write costs the connection and only a browser restores it.
- Resource binding is mandatory, or the token is audienced elsewhere and every
  call returns 401 looking valid.

The public API is deliberately synchronous. A scheduled job has no event loop
and no host, and a test keeps it that way, because quietly returning coroutines
would revert this to a source that only works inside a session.

The sweep distinguishes unreachable from empty, which is the failure the whole
design exists to remove: an outage must never be reported as a quiet week. It
leaves unfinalized captures alone, since a partial note would never be revisited,
and survives a single bad capture rather than ending the run.

The setup skill states two things a user would otherwise discover late: captures
from this source may carry no attendee names, and the credential sits in the
vault and needs excluding from backups the way .env already is.

Verified against a live account: dynamic registration, PKCE, refresh and the MCP
client all work, and four real captures were fetched, written, attributed
against the calendar where it could confirm them, and correctly skipped on a
second run.

The credential store here is local. It should move behind the connection manager
once that can hold a public client registered on the fly, which is the subject
of a separate change.

Part of #564. The learning file on this vault contained nothing but its own
header for two consecutive days, while the autocommit hook faithfully committed
it and every mechanism reported success.

Two faults, both silent.

The transcript path was read from "$1", and settings.json passes
"$transcript_path" -- a shell variable nothing in the hook environment ever
sets, so it expanded to empty on every real invocation. Hooks receive their
payload as JSON on stdin; soft-promise-detector.py already does this. Stdin is
now the primary source, with argv kept as a fallback because the harness
invokes the hook directly.

The whole session record was then gated on that path being present. But the
valuable part -- that a session ended, and when -- does not depend on it.
Gating the essential on the optional turned a broken input contract into a file
that reads as a quiet day. The record is now written unconditionally, and
whether the transcript could be located is reported as part of it, in the three
distinguishable states: found, named but absent, or never supplied.

It also stops promising extraction it cannot deliver. The old text said "Run
/daily-review to extract learnings from this session" in every case, including
the ones where no transcript exists to extract from.

settings.json is deliberately untouched. The "$transcript_path" argument is now
redundant rather than harmful, and removing it is a separate tidy-up that would
collide with other work on that file.

Six tests: stdin payload, no transcript, path present but file absent, argv
fallback, the day file never left header-only, and repeat sessions appending
rather than replacing.

Meeting prep builds the brief without refreshing the meeting record (#592)

* Refresh the meeting record before building a prep brief

/meeting-prep reads 00-Inbox/Meetings at Step 3 and never refreshes it.
/daily-plan and /daily-review both run /process-meetings first; meeting-prep
is the only one of the three that does not, and it is the one most likely to
need the refresh.

It is normally run minutes before a call, which is exactly when the most
recent conversation with those attendees is most likely to still be sitting
unprocessed at the source. A brief built from a stale folder does not look
incomplete. It looks like there was nothing to report, which is the same
output as a genuinely quiet history. Missing context and no context are
indistinguishable to the reader.

Adds Step 0 (the same refresh daily-plan uses, same silent-if-nothing-found
handling, same no-rating-for-a-sub-step rule), renumbers the old Step 0 to
0.5, and notes the dependency at Step 3 where it actually bites.

The test asserts ORDER, not presence: a refresh that happens after the read
is too late to affect the brief. Parameterised across the three briefing
skills so the next one added inherits the contract. It fails on meeting-prep
against the unpatched tree and passes for the other two either way.

* Say what process-meetings actually refreshes

The Step 0 wording said it "pulls anything unprocessed from the
meeting source", which reads as though the step reaches out to an
external recorder and syncs. It does not. It processes captures
already sitting in the local meeting folder.

Reworded to promise the freshest locally available record, and to
say plainly that anything not yet synced from an external source
stays out of reach either way. The gap this step actually closes is
between a capture landing locally and it being readable here, which
is still the gap that matters minutes before a call.

Re-state the time on every prompt, so a long session cannot lose the date (#566)

* Re-state the time on every prompt, so a long session cannot lose the date

Context carries no freshness. Everything in it presents with equal authority
whether it was observed a minute ago or yesterday, so the date printed once at
session start sits there unchanged and unqualified for as long as the session
lasts.

In a short session that is harmless. In a long one it is the cause of a specific
failure, observed on a real vault: SessionStart printed Tuesday's date, the
session ran overnight, and on Wednesday morning a full daily plan was built,
presented and defended as "today's" using Tuesday. Nothing in context
contradicted it, because the stale line and a fresh one look identical.

The hook is deliberately unconditional. Emitting only on change would be
cheaper, but every conditional hook in this tree is a place where a branch can
quietly not fire, and this file exists because of that class of bug. One date
call per prompt is not worth being clever about.

The day-change line is the part that earns its keep: crossing midnight
mid-session is the moment context stops being merely old and becomes wrong, so
that transition is stated once rather than left to be noticed.

Wired first on UserPromptSubmit, ahead of the hooks that reason, so the clock is
established before anything uses it. Any failure is silent and exits 0: a vault
that cannot read a clock is no worse off than before.

Context in #565.

The most reusable signal about how an assistant fails is the moment its user
says so. Today that signal reaches nothing durable: extraction lives in

even on a bad day.

ordinary instructions from one session, eight of nine corrections are caught
with one false positive ("I have no preference, pick one"). The miss is "what

Restack knowledge half-life onto current main (#569) (#744)

* Proposal: declare how long an observation stays trustworthy, and measure it

Concrete basis for the discussion in #565, deliberately not wired into any
skill. The design decisions worth arguing about are which artefacts require
what, and that should be settled before anything enforces it.

The problem: context carries no freshness marker. A calendar read from four
hours ago and one from a minute ago sit side by side with identical authority,
which is how a long session ends up using yesterday's date, an unchecked inbox,
and a stale task list while sounding entirely current.

Three pieces.

**A per-vault declaration** (System/knowledge-half-life.yaml, shipped as seed so
user tuning is never overwritten). Volatility is personal: one person's pipeline
moves weekly, another's task list hourly, so a fixed table ships wrong for most
people. Sources that do not decay are declared `never`, because a user's
decisions and corrections are superseded rather than aged out.

**Observations recorded mechanically.** A PostToolUse hook stamps a source the
moment a tool that reads it is called. This is the part that matters: an
assistant that cannot notice its context has gone stale is exactly the one that
will forget to record when it last looked, so self-reporting would inherit the
original defect. The ledger reflects what happened, not what was believed.

**An artefact contract**, which is the half that can honestly be enforced. An
assistant cannot audit its own memory for staleness, but "a daily plan requires
a calendar read newer than its half-life" is checkable from outside. On this
vault, run against yesterday's daily plan, it returns exactly the failure that
occurred: email STALE at 240 minutes, week_priorities NOT OBSERVED.

Distinctions the module refuses to collapse, each of which has already caused a
real failure somewhere in this codebase: a missing config is UNAVAILABLE rather
than everything-is-fresh; a typo in a half-life fails loudly rather than
silently becoming fresh-forever; an unknown source gets the cautious answer; and
"stale" reads differently from "never observed" because they call for different
responses.

18 tests. All twelve quality gates pass.

* Starter for the learning routing step: parse, cluster, propose, record

Offered against #503, to @joshm-simril's design and @davekilleen's spec. The
routing table is Josh's, kept as data rather than code so it can be edited
without touching this module, which was one of his own open questions.

Deliberately does NOT apply anything. Dex must never silently rewrite its own
instructions, so the edit has to be shown and confirmed before it lands, and
confirmation belongs in the skill that can hold a conversation. Everything here
is analysis and bookkeeping.

The split is the point: clustering and destination-proposal are mechanical and
testable, while deciding whether a proposed edit is right is judgement. Mixing
them would bury an unreviewable decision inside something that looks like a
helper.

Four pieces, matching the spec on #503:

- Parse entries from Session_Learnings with enough location to rewrite one
  status without disturbing its neighbours.
- Cluster by proposed destination rather than by wording, because two entries
  belonging in the same file are worth reviewing together even when they read
  differently. Josh's observation was that eight related entries became one
  rule, not eight edits.
- Trigger on volume OR age. Age matters independently: a single correction left
  for a fortnight is a worse signal than ten from this morning, and a count-only
  trigger never fires on a slow, steady leak.
- Record an outcome as implemented (date and destination) or dropped (date and
  reason), so a falling count means something was installed rather than
  something ageing out of view. An invented third status is refused.

14 tests, including that two entries in one file can never have their statuses
crossed. All twelve quality gates pass.

Restack #590: make the feature-adoption log reachable after the learning stack (#743)

* Make the feature-adoption log actually record what you use

usage_log.md drives /dex-level-up: it records which Dex features a vault has
used so the skill can recommend the ones it has not. mark_feature_used() is
the documented way to record that, and it could not do it.

Three separate reasons, each of which alone would be enough:

1. It was never exposed as a tool. The only documented caller is a skill,
   and skills reach Python through MCP. The function has lived in
   analytics_helper.py unreachable from the place the checklist tells authors
   to call it from.

2. Its pattern could not match most of the file. The label matcher used
   [^(\\n]* around the feature name, which stops at the first bracket, so any
   entry written as "Daily planning (\`/daily-plan\`)" was unmatchable. On a
   real vault that is 37 of 61 remaining features.

3. It returned None whether it worked or not. A caller could not tell a
   successful tick from a no-op, so a miss looked exactly like a hit. That is
   why the drift was invisible: the log on the vault this was found on had not
   changed in twelve days while the features were in daily use.

This replaces the matcher with an ordered one (slash command, then exact
label, then label with the command stripped), returns a status instead of
None, refuses to guess when several entries match, and writes through a temp
file so an interrupted write cannot truncate the consent records that share
this file.

Adoption tracking is deliberately NOT gated on analytics consent, and there
is a test for that: it writes to the vault and sends nothing, and the
recommendations it feeds are useful whether or not a user shares anything.

The parsed feature map in load_usage_log() had no consumers, so the read side
was dead too. A test now covers the loop end to end.

* Move the adoption-log write behind a lifecycle operation

Review of #590: mark_feature_used wrote System/usage_log.md directly, which
breaks Dex's vault-mutation contract and is unsafe three ways. All three
reproduce against the old approach and are now covered by tests:

- a vault whose System directory is a symlink had the write land outside the
  vault entirely;
- a 0600 log became 0644, because write_text on a fresh temporary takes the
  umask and the rename carries it;
- the fixed .tmp sibling is the same path for both writers, so a feature tick
  and a consent update could each read, modify and write the whole file and
  silently lose the other's change.

Adds rewrite_usage_log() to core/lifecycle/service.py, modelled on the
existing analytics-receipt seam: whole-route symlink validation before the
file is read, a refusal on a symlinked target, bounded read, expected-SHA
guard with stale retry, and the existing mode re-stated in the plan so a
write can never loosen it.

Scoped by the contract rather than by the caller. The new usage-log operation
is authorised for exactly one path, so it cannot write anything else even if
a future caller asks it to, and the bounded-read limit is registered at both
engine sites.

update_consent now uses the same door, per the review: with two direct
writers the concurrency guarantee would not have been real.

The MCP helper keeps its matching and its five statuses. It decides the
outcome from a plain read so a no-op never opens a transaction, and its
transform re-matches against the text the transaction actually read, because
a retry may run it again after another writer has ticked the same box.

Dex times its own rituals and stops turning meeting remarks into tasks (release v1.97.20) (#747)

Ritual clock
- New hook `.claude/hooks/ritual-timing.py` (thin wrapper over
  `core/utils/ritual_timing.py`) wired on PreToolUse:Skill (start),
  Stop (a hand-back closes a working stretch; the first is
  time-to-first-hand-back), UserPromptSubmit (the person replied, Dex is
  working again), PreToolUse:mcp__.*__track_event (the rituals'
  `*_completed` analytics event closes the run as completed when it
  arrives) and SessionEnd.
- Two readings per run: time to first hand-back, which needs no end
  signal, and Dex's working time, the sum of prompt-to-hand-back
  stretches. Time waiting on the person is recorded separately and never
  judged, so walking away mid-plan is not a slow plan.
- The completion event is a bonus, not a requirement: without it a run
  ends, marked inferred, when the next skill starts in the session or the
  session ends. A run cut off before any hand-back is abandoned and never
  judged. The meeting pass still nests inside the plan and review after a
  question. Same-skill restarts supersede the unfinished run.
- Events append to `System/.dex/ritual-timings.jsonl`; in-flight runs live
  in `System/.dex/ritual-timing-active.json` keyed by session, with a
  24-hour TTL. Both paths are new `core.paths` constants. Every record
  carries the Dex version and the SKILL.md sha256 at run time.
- The hook command tolerates a machine without python3 on PATH (exit 0,

fix(learning): strip harness text before spotting corrections, in both spotters (#770)

Both correction spotters read text the harness writes into a user turn as if
the user had written it. The live hook's gate greps the raw payload, and
correction-capture.py recorded whatever passed without re-testing it, so a
reminder, task notification or CI event that happened to contain "wrong",
"stop" or "don't" was filed as the user's correction, alongside whatever the
user actually typed ("run the daily plan"). The new session-end extractor had
no filter at all, and also re-read compaction summaries, which quote the
user's earlier corrections back as a user turn.

One rule now, in both places: remove machine text first (any lowercase tag
with a hyphen, closed or running to the end; a short list of untagged
preambles; compaction-summary records), then test the correction wording on
what is left. A real correction sent alongside a reminder is still recorded,
with only the user's words. <pasted_content> is kept, since a pasted
correction can be the user's own.

On one long real transcript the session-end extractor went from 10
machine-generated candidates out of 73 to none out of 65, with the real
corrections unchanged.

Co-authored-by: Chris Jackson <201591867+chrisjackson-coding@users.noreply.github.com>
Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(doctor): measure Apple Mail index freshness from the newest sync, not the oldest mailbox (#771)

The Apple Mail search check reports BROKEN ("older than the configured
24-hour freshness limit") on a healthy index whenever any one mailbox has
been quiet for a day, and stays BROKEN while search returns current mail.

apple-mail-mcp stamps sync_state.last_sync only on mailboxes whose mail
changed in that sync, and writes a ("_global", "_sync") row when a sync ran
and nothing changed (apple_mail_mcp/index/sync.py). So a per-mailbox
last_sync records when that mailbox last changed, not when it was last
checked. Taking the oldest one means a quiet Junk or Deleted Items folder
crosses the limit and never comes back. apple-mail-mcp's own index status
measures staleness as MAX(last_sync) over the same table.

A sync is a single pass over the whole mail store, so freshness is now the
newest last_sync in sync_state. The requirement that every indexed mailbox
has at least one successful sync is kept unchanged, as is its test case.
The mixed-fresh-and-stale case is replaced by tests for a quiet mailbox, a
no-change sync, and an index where no sync has run within the limit.
